lessons.title: Numbers 0â100 and Phone Numbers
lessons.body:

Phone numbers are crucial for business in Africa. In Mandarin, you read each digit separately. For example, 0712345678 becomes lÃ­ng qÄ« yÄ« Ã¨r sÄn sÃ¬ wÇ liÃ¹ qÄ« bÄ. Note: 0 is often read as 'dÃ²ng' in phone numbers (from 'zero' in English), but 'lÃ­ng' is also fine. Practice with your own number: write it down, then say each digit in Mandarin. Use numbers in prices: 50 shillings = wÇshÃ­ xiÄnlÃ¬ng. 1000 naira = yÄ«qiÄn nÃ ilÄ. In markets, bargaining is common. Say 'tÃ i guÃ¬ le' (too expensive) and offer a lower price: 'sÄnshÃ­ kuÃ i, xÃ­ng ma?' (30 yuan, okay?). Learn to understand numbers quickly when spoken. Listen to Chinese media or use apps like HelloChinese to drill numbers. Practice with a partner: one says a number in Mandarin, the other writes it down. Do this daily for 10 minutes.

For phone numbers, remember that Chinese mobile numbers are 11 digits, often starting with 1. But in Africa, you'll use local numbers. The key is to be able to say and understand any sequence. lessons.title: Days of the Week and Months
lessons.body:
In Mandarin, days of the week are easy: they are 'week' (xÄ«ngqÄ«) plus a number. Monday is xÄ«ngqÄ«yÄ« (week one), Tuesday xÄ«ngqÄ«'Ã¨r, Wednesday xÄ«ngqÄ«sÄn, Thursday xÄ«ngqÄ«sÃ¬, Friday xÄ«ngqÄ«wÇ, Saturday xÄ«ngqÄ«liÃ¹, and Sunday is xÄ«ngqÄ«tiÄn or xÄ«ngqÄ«rÃ¬ (week day/sun). So if you know numbers 1â6, you know the days. Practice by saying the day for each date on a calendar. For example, if today is Tuesday, say 'jÄ«ntiÄn xÄ«ngqÄ«'Ã¨r'.

Months are even simpler: they are 'month' (yuÃ¨) plus a number. January is yÄ«yuÃ¨ (one month), February Ã¨ryuÃ¨, March sÄnyuÃ¨, April sÃ¬yuÃ¨, May wÇyuÃ¨, June liÃ¹yuÃ¨, July qÄ«yuÃ¨, August bÄyuÃ¨, September jiÇyuÃ¨, October shÃ­yuÃ¨, November shÃ­yÄ«yuÃ¨, December shÃ­'Ã¨ryuÃ¨. So you only need to know numbers 1â12. Practice by listing the months in order, then saying your birthday month.

To say 'today is Monday', say 'jÄ«ntiÄn xÄ«ngqÄ«yÄ«'. For 'tomorrow is Tuesday', say 'mÃ­ngtiÄn xÄ«ngqÄ«'Ã¨r'. For 'yesterday was Sunday', say 'zuÃ³tiÄn xÄ«ngqÄ«tiÄn'. These phrases are useful for scheduling. In Africa, many business meetings are set by day and date. If someone says 'meet on Friday', you can confirm: 'xÄ«ngqÄ«wÇ, duÃ¬ ma?' (Friday, right?).

Also learn to ask 'what day is it today?' â 'jÄ«ntiÄn xÄ«ngqÄ«jÇ?' (Today is what day of the week?). The answer will be one of the days. Similarly, ask 'what month is it?' â 'xiÃ nzÃ i shÃ¬ jÇ yuÃ¨?' (Now is what month?). Practice with a friend: ask and answer these questions daily. Use a Chinese calendar app or write the days and months in your notebook. Repetition will make them automatic.

In business, knowing days and months helps with planning. For example, 'wÇmen xÄ«ngqÄ«sÄn jiÃ nmiÃ n' (We meet on Wednesday). 'SÄnyuÃ¨ shÃ­wÇ rÃ¬ shÃ¬ jiÃ©zhÃ¬ rÃ¬qÄ«' (March 15 is the deadline). lessons.title: Telling Time: Hours and Minutes

To tell time in Mandarin, use 'diÇn' for hour and 'fÄn' for minutes. The structure is: number + diÇn + number + fÄn. For example, 3:00 is sÄn diÇn. 3:15 is sÄn diÇn shÃ­wÇ fÄn. 3:30 is sÄn diÇn sÄnshÃ­ fÄn, but more commonly sÄn diÇn bÃ n (half past three). 3:45 is sÄn diÇn sÃ¬shÃ­wÇ fÄn. For 'a.m.' and 'p.m.', use 'shÃ ngwÇ' (morning, before noon) and 'xiÃ wÇ' (afternoon, after noon). So 9:00 a.m. is shÃ ngwÇ jiÇ diÇn. 2:00 p.m. is xiÃ wÇ liÇng diÇn. Note: 2 o'clock is 'liÇng diÇn', not 'Ã¨r diÇn', when telling time.

To ask 'what time is it?', say 'xiÃ nzÃ i jÇ diÇn?' (Now what time?). The answer: 'xiÃ nzÃ i sÄn diÇn shÃ­wÇ fÄn' (Now 3:15). For 'what time do you...?', say 'nÇ jÇ diÇn...?' For example, 'nÇ jÇ diÇn qÇchuÃ¡ng?' (What time do you get up?). Practice answering with your daily routine: 'wÇ qÄ« diÇn qÇchuÃ¡ng' (I get up at 7). 'WÇ bÄ diÇn chÄ« zÇofÃ n' (I eat breakfast at 8). 'WÇ jiÇ diÇn shÃ ngbÄn' (I start work at 9).

In Africa, punctuality varies, but in business, being on time is appreciated. If you have a meeting at 10:30, say 'shÃ­ diÇn bÃ n'. If it's 10:45, say 'shÃ­ diÇn sÃ¬shÃ­wÇ fÄn' or 'chÃ  shÃ­wÇ fÄn shÃ­yÄ« diÇn' (15 minutes to 11). The latter is less common but useful to understand. Also learn 'bÃ n' (half), 'kÃ¨' (quarter, 15 minutes). So 10:15 is 'shÃ­ diÇn yÄ« kÃ¨' or 'shÃ­ diÇn shÃ­wÇ fÄn'. 10:45 is 'shÃ­ diÇn sÄn kÃ¨' or 'chÃ  yÄ« kÃ¨ shÃ­yÄ« diÇn'.

Practice with a clock or phone. Set random times and say them in Mandarin. Use a timer: every hour, say the time aloud. When scheduling, confirm times: 'wÇmen liÇng diÇn jiÃ n, xÃ­ng ma?' lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Numbers, Dates, and Time in Mandarin for African Agribusiness

In cross-border agribusiness, a single misunderstood number can cost a shipment, a contract, or a season. Whether you are negotiating the price of cashew in Abidjan, confirming a cold-chain pickup in Nairobi, or scheduling a buyer call in Guangzhou, Mandarin numbers, dates, and time expressions are operational tools â not academic trivia. This Practical Reference consolidates the module into a working desk guide for African traders, exporters, cooperative managers, and logistics officers who deal with Chinese suppliers, buyers, and freight forwarders.

Chinese numbers are highly regular, which is good news for busy professionals. Once you learn 0â100, you can form phone numbers, prices, quantities, ages, and dates. The main traps are tone changes, the liÇng vs. Ã¨r distinction for "two," and the fact that Chinese dates run from largest unit to smallest (year â month â day), the opposite of many African and European conventions. Master these and you remove most scheduling errors before they happen.

For African exporters, the highest-value application of numbers is the phone number. Chinese business cards, WeChat profiles, and freight documents list numbers in digit strings. Read them digit by digit. Note that in phone numbers, yÄ« (1) is usually pronounced yÄo to avoid confusion with qÄ« (7). So +86 138 0013 8000 is read "yÄo sÄn bÄ, lÃ­ng lÃ­ng yÄo sÄn, bÄ lÃ­ng lÃ­ng lÃ­ng." Practise reading your own Kenyan, Nigerian, Ghanaian, or South African number aloud in Mandarin so you can dictate it to a Chinese counterpart without error.

When you confirm a shipment date, always write the full Chinese form in the contract or email, then repeat it verbally. This single habit prevents the classic "03/04" dispute that has delayed many cocoa, coffee, and sesame consignments.

"ä¸åä¸ç¹" is 3 p.m. Because China Standard Time is UTC+8, a 3 p.m. Beijing call is 10 a.m. in Nairobi (UTC+3), 9 a.m. in Lagos (UTC+1), and 7 a.m. in Accra (UTC+0). Always state the time zone in writing, and repeat the Chinese time aloud to confirm.

Never confirm a payment amount, bank account number, or contract date by voice alone in a language you are still learning. Numbers such as 4 (sÃ¬) and 10 (shÃ­), or 1 (yÄ«) and 7 (qÄ«), are easily misheard on poor mobile connections common in rural sourcing areas. Always follow up with a written message (WeChat, email, or SMS) showing the digits and the full date in both Chinese and your local format. For payments, verify the beneficiary account through an independent channel before transfer. Fraudsters exploit language gaps and time-zone pressure â slow down and double-check.

Business-hour norms vary by sector and are drawn from common trade practice reported by the International Trade Centre (ITC) and national chambers of commerce.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Read phone numbers digit by digit and say 1 as yÄo, not yÄ«.
  • Use ä¸¤ (liÇng) before measure words (tonnes, containers, kilograms), not äº (Ã¨r).
  • Write dates as å¹´ â æ â æ¥ in all contracts and emails to remove ambiguity.
  • State the time zone every time you book a call; Beijing is UTC+8.
  • Confirm numbers in writing after every voice call, especially payments and account details.
  • Use ä¸å / ä¸å / æä¸ to avoid a.m./p.m. confusion.

  • Repeat back the date, time, quantity, and price your counterpart states, then ask å¯¹å? (correct?).

  • HSK Official Test Centre â syllabus and vocabulary lists including numbers and time
  • IANA Time Zone Database â authoritative time-zone reference for Africa and China
  • International Trade Centre â trade documentation and cross-border business guides
  • African Union â regional trade and AfCFTA resources for exporters

Used daily, this reference turns Mandarin from a barrier into a competitive advantage. African agribusinesses that can confirm a container count, a harvest date, and a payment time in clear Mandarin close deals faster and with fewer disputes. Keep this page open during calls, and build the habit of written confirmation after every conversation.
